question: Enel Green Power’s Monte Amiata (Tuscany) geothermal facilities use flash technology and produce emissions that contain similar – and sometimes higher – quantities of greenhouse gases than fossil fuel-fired electrical plants1. These geothermal facilities also emit significant quantities of ammonia, hydrogen sulphide, mercury and other substances harmful to public health and the environment.

A supporter of the current model of local geothermal development, the Tuscany Regional Executive recently agreed to extend the aforementioned Enel concessions by another 20 years2. However, the Regional Health Agency (ARS) has reported that male mortality rates in the local area have long outstripped normal levels by a significant margin3.

Acknowledging that geothermal production is not always clean, Recital 46 of Directive (EU) 2018/2001 states that ‘the Commission should therefore facilitate only the deployment of geothermal energy with a low environmental impact and resulting in greenhouse gas emissions savings.
’ There are ways of generating geothermal energy without releasing greenhouse gases or producing emissions of any kind, a case in point being Eavor’s closed-loop technology4.

In the light of the situation regarding the Monte Amiata geothermal power plants, could the Commission clarify whether it will draft guidelines that can steer stakeholders towards new geothermal technologies that have a low environmental impact and whether it will allocate dedicated funds or propose legislative measures to this effect?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2026) The Commission acknowledges that geothermal energy plays an important role in the decarbonisation of the EU. A Commission study1 analysed the emissions of geothermal plants across Europe and concluded that extreme values are typically linked to specific locations and older plants. Most of the systems operate in closed loops, where no relevant emissions occur.

Geothermal projects are covered by EU environmental legislation. Under the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive2, geothermal projects that may significantly affect the environment must undergo an environmental assessment before approval; it requires authorities to assess impacts on air quality, climate and human health.

To facilitate the environmental assessments, the Commission proposed in the European Grids Package3 that Member States set up single digital portals that ensure access to all relevant environmental and geological data for permit-granting procedures.

Furthermore, as set out in the AccelerateEU Communication4, the Commission will support Member States and stakeholders in gathering detailed geological data and create an EU-level database as well as showcase best practices for clean technologies.

The Commission also supports research and development in geothermal technologies to improve the environmental performance, such as the project for geothermal emissions control under Horizon 20205 that also included consortium partners from Italy.

Geothermal projects reducing greenhouse gas emissions are also supported under the Innovation Fund and in general, in EU Funding calls, the inclusion of the ‘do no significant harm’ principle as an eligibility condition reinforces environmental compliance across all topics.
